analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators fine insurers and employers that shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late June 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has seen no further action and has one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires health plans to cover mental health and addiction care on equal terms with physical health care, but the Labor Department has long had no direct way to fine plans that violate that rule. This bill would let federal regulators impose civil monetary penalties on plan sponsors, insurers, and administrators that shortchange mental health benefits, and it would give the Labor Department's benefits agency $30 million a year for five years to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-based health insurance who need mental health or substance use care. If enforced, they would face fewer denials, higher reimbursement, and fewer restrictive limits on therapy, inpatient stays, and addiction treatment. The bill also gives enforcers dedicated funding, which makes the parity rules easier to police in practice.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds civil monetary penalties under ERISA for failing to meet the parity requirements of the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, extending liability to plan sponsors, service providers, and plan administrators [S2].
It carves out an exception so the Labor Secretary can directly enforce the mental health parity section, a pathway that does not otherwise exist in the statute [S2].
It appropriates $30 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 to the Employee Benefits Security Administration to carry out parity enforcement [S2].
The changes apply to plan years beginning more than one year after enactment, giving plans time to comply [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Group health plan sponsors (usually employers), health insurers, and plan administrators, who would face fines and stronger compliance requirements, and taxpayers, who fund the new $30 million annual appropriation. Some of the compliance cost could flow into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Civil monetary penalties and tighter enforcement raise compliance costs for employers who sponsor health plans, and some of that cost can be passed to workers through premiums or reduced benefits [S2].
The bill appropriates $30 million a year in new federal spending for five years, adding roughly $150 million to the cost of enforcement [S2].

In the short run, stronger parity enforcement can mean insurers tighten medical-necessity reviews or narrow other benefits to absorb the cost of expanded mental health payment, so gains may take time to show up for patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers whose mental health or addiction claims are quietly paid less or denied more than comparable medical claims, real fines and a funded enforcer could change behavior in a way that two decades of unfunded parity rules have not. The cost side is modest: employer compliance spending and a $30 million annual appropriation. The main honest caveat is that penalties only matter if the enforcer uses them, and a $30 million budget for a national enforcement job is not large.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not taken it up, so it sits at the very first step of the process with months left in the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Kean Jr. introduced the bill in the House on June 30, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the Committee on Education and Workforce [S1][S2].
The action history shows no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S4].
The bill has a single cosponsor, a Republican, matching the sponsor's party [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has moved: employers and insurers face no new penalties, and patients have no new enforcement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: insurers and employers unaffected

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

for.name: Unnamed House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor are both Republicans; no one has acted against the bill, but it has not drawn bipartisan support either.

industries.note: The bill exposes insurers to federal fines if their mental health coverage fails parity tests, and lets the Labor Department enforce directly. Their interest in avoiding fines and denying or underpaying mental health claims runs against patients who need that care.
Employers who self-insure would face liability for parity failures and new compliance costs. Their cost can be real, though the same rules aim to guarantee the coverage their workers already pay for.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Stronger parity enforcement means fewer claim denials and better payment for therapy, psychiatric care, and addiction treatment, expanding access for patients and revenue for providers.

analysis.trajectory: A bill introduced at the very end of a two-year Congress with one cosponsor and no committee action almost never reaches a floor vote. It would need the Education and Workforce Committee to schedule a markup and the House leadership to schedule floor time, neither of which is likely in the remaining months unless parity enforcement becomes a broader priority.
